title: Crucial Conversations Book Summary: How to Make It Safe to Talk About Anything
transcript: I recently listened to Crucial Conversations on audio and honestly I did not expect that much out of it I thought it would be this short behavior based communication skill book and instead I found it full of depth on how to improve difficult conversations. In this summary I'm going to share the essence of how Crucial Conversations teaches you to have good dialogue by making it safe to talk about anything, and I'm gonna share the five most important things I learned from Crucial Conversations. Now like I said I didn't  expect much out of this book I  thought it would be another skills based approach that teaches the right words to say to basically manipulate others into doing what you want. But in the long run that approach I don't believe is very effective. So I went into this book not really expecting much of it and instead I found a depth of theory that from my therapy perspective was half way between Sue Johnson's emotion focused therapy and John Gottman's approach which include things like seven principles for making marriage work and the four horsemen and etc. So from my totally therapy centered approach I saw this book is all about creating safety so that problems could be solved. Because this book goes deeper than behavior I think it offers real solutions to improving relationships and managing intensely emotional conversations. So let's jump in to some of the essential skills. So the first one is remember your goal. So this first skill is to continually remind yourself of your goal which is to share a conversation and to solve a problem and not allow yourself to get sidetracked by switching goals. So a lot of times we get caught up in contention like needing to be right needing to win needing to punish others needing to be justified. So instead this book encourages you to keep in mind the question what do I want for myself and for others and for the relationship. So for example when having a discussion with a teenager about curfew instead of getting locked up in what time they have to be home continually remind yourself and them that what you really want is for them to be safe and for you to be able to trust them to be responsible. They also want to be trusted and seen as responsible because that comes with freedoms. So that shared goal of mutual trust can get you on the same team as you work to figure out what time they should be home. Number two, watch for signs of stress. So learn to look for signs of crucial conversations and signs of stress within yourself. When you notice yourself getting heated take a deep breath actively calm yourself and remind yourself to stick to the goal which is shared dialogue and shared meaning. This step is basically learning to be responsive instead of reactive to the situation. Number three, give yourself more options. So let go of false dichotomies. In therapy we call this black-and-white thinking. So for example I either had to let the boss walk all over me or I had to rudely embarrass him. I had to say nothing or I would lose my job. So instead of these dichotomies instead of you know this black-and-white thinking, you ask yourself to step back and really consider, are there truly no other options is there anyone in the company who uses a different strategy or approach for dealing with that situation? And your goal is to relax a little bit and invite creativity and flexibility. My dad once told me the story of a college president who during the Vietnam War he was struggling to know how to deal with the protesters on his campus. He had one group who wanted to burn the American flag to show their anger about the draft and the war and he had the football team who was surrounding the flag to protect it. As tensions were rising violence seemed imminent and in similar situations other universities sent in riot police or the National Guard and this led to escalating tension and injuries and deaths. But this university president stepped back took a look at the situation and made an offer. What if we wash the flag. A symbolic move that both shows respect and the need for improvement and because of his willingness to look for that third option the situation was resolved peacefully. Number four, check how you see others. This was my number one take away. Whenever someone reverts to silence like shutting down withdrawing going quiet or violence like aggression raising their voice or arguing. Our natural reaction is to respond more forcefully arguing our point or getting frustrated that they won't participate and instead this book challenges us to see silence or violence as a sign that the other person isn't feeling safe to talk. They feel like their point isn't being considered and they get into a fight or flight mode. When we see this we have to stop ourselves and ask what can I do to restore safety? Crucial Conversations suggest some practical steps to restoring safety. So they need to know that you care about them and their interests so show them respect check yourself am I listening am I validating am I acting defensive or being condescending or sarcastic? Am I showing them that I value hearing what they are saying even if I don't agree? Now I think this step is really powerful because we can actively create a safe environment by how we treat the other person. When people feel that you care about them and value them it invites them to relax and be able to absorb what you're saying and share what they need to. So it makes it more likely that you'll have a successful conversation that actually solves problems. Number five, creating safety a big part to restoring safety is working on yourself. But there are some other skills that are pretty straightforward to help others feel safe understood and valued. So one of these is front-loading. This is starting off conversations gently when a topic is crucial we tend to get nervous and go into it like tightly after avoiding it for a while so instead lead in gently. For example, there's something I'd like to get your opinion on but I'm worried that you'll be upset if I bring it up. Front loading can help a conversation go better right from the start. Here's another one, point out you agree on highlight the areas you share instead of only focusing on the parts you disagree with. Keep pointing out your common goal for example, I really want to be able to work well with you this relationship is more important or let's see how we can solve this in a way that everyone can accept. If you need to make a tentative guess about what they're feeling upset about but not in a judgmental way. So for example you could say, it sounds like you're feeling like your opinion isn't being heard. Number six, master your stories. So this sixth chapter on mastering your stories it's like this combination of the book leadership and self-deception and narrative therapy and a little bit of CBT thrown in for good measure. But basically it tries to help you see when you're interpreting situations in a way that harms the process. Stories are our assumptions of why people are doing what they're doing. For example, seeing yourself as the victim or blaming others as being lazy or selfish are types of stories that we tell ourselves. Distorting the facts by exaggerating their wrongs or highlighting their strengths is why these stories become problematic. Now I thought this chapter was on point but to me it feels like a couple of books worth of information in one short chapter. So I wonder if people are actually able to absorb it in small doses or if it is better addressed in more depth. Regardless you should check yourself for signs of this. Do you have repeating patterns at work like why is everyone out to get me or all bosses are authoritarian a-holes or I'm the only hard worker around here. When you see your underlying stories for what they are, stories, then you can see past them and solve real problems. Try to replace defensiveness with curiosity. This is something that I struggle with and this book frames this in an interesting way, when faced with someone who seems to be getting angry shutting down or being irrational rather than ask what's the worst most personal way I can take this which leads to defensiveness we should ask why would a reasonable rational and decent person think or feel this way? Leading to curiosity it's hard to feel defensive and curious at the same time. Assuming that they're doing the best they can can help us understand their obstacles to having a dialogue around crucial issues. When it comes down to it what I appreciated most about this book was its emphasis on creating real safety by giving me the responsibility to create that safe environment and it teaches the tools to make that happen. Thanks for watching and if you found this content helpful please consider sharing it with someone who also might find it helpful. Take care.

title: Crucial Conversations Summary & Review (ANIMATED)
transcript: In this episode, you're going to get a summary of  the book Crucial Conversations. It is by far one   of the best books that I've read on interpersonal  communication, on what do you do when the   stakes are that high, when you know that this  conversation is going to change your life. Whether   that's a personal, business, it does not matter.  What are you doing in those super important   conversations? Let me show you what this book  is all about. Let's talk about the core ideas,   and then let's jump into what do you do, how do  you implement them in your life? Let's do it.   Close your eyes and imagine the most average  person you can think of. Well, that's James.   He's a regular guy with an ordinary life. He loves  books, the Beatles, and spending time with his   girlfriend. He loves to spend his weekend on the  couch, watching TV. And today is a typical day,   a Saturday like any other in James' life, or at  least it was until the moment his girlfriend,   Anna, comes home and says, "We need to talk."  James is caught off guard. His stress levels   increase drastically and he cannot reason. With  no prior warning, James finds himself in a crucial   conversation that will undoubtedly shape his  immediate future and his relationship.   A crucial conversation is a discussion  which is typically characterized   by three major factors. Stakes are high, opinions  vary, and the parties involved have strong   emotions. And we've all had at least a few of  those in our lives, even if we didn't realize   it at the time. And make no mistake, crucial  conversation is not a planned high-level   meeting like the one you might have at work during  let's say your scheduled yearly manager meeting.   Crucial conversations are things like ending a  relationship, giving your boss critical but needed   feedback, or something like confronting a coworker  or a neighbor about something that they did.   The problem with such high stake  conversations is that we often plain suck at   having them. We tend to avoid these conversations  because we're afraid we're going to make matters   worse. We tend to react negatively when put into  a crucial conversation, for the simple reason that   we're human, and human beings tend to behave their  worst in the most critical moment, as the author   puts it herself. After all, when you're under  stress, blood is directed away from your brain   into your muscles, so your thinking naturally  suffers. You're also most likely caught off guard,   so your first reaction might even surprise you  when you analyze it later on. Plus, you're lacking   the right tools to handle such conversation. After  all, crucial conversations 101 is not something   that is taught in schools or university. You've  got to figure out stuff by yourself. So let's   fix all this and arm you with the right skills  needed to handle any crucial conversation, because   eventually you're going to find yourself in one,  or you have to deliver one, no doubt about it.   It all starts with knowing your heart. First and  foremost, you absolutely need to stay focused on   what you really want in a conversation, and none  of the petty BS stuff like winning the argument,   but the big picture item, like having a  stronger relationship or a better job.   Of course, this is not easy, and you might  need to reverse some of the tactics that   you grew up with, such as silent treatment or  manipulation, or having to quote unquote win.   You're not in a competitive sport, so  winning the conversation might mean losing   the relationship. So always keep that in mind.  Avoid trying to discredit the other person or   put them in their place, as they say, as those,  again, put you away from the original purpose.   Remember what you really want. If the other party  says something you disagree with, take a pause,   remind yourself of what you really want, reboot,  and get back into conversation. Uncomfortable?   For sure, but exponentially better than going  on the offense with a knee jerk reaction.   Next, you absolutely need to ensure safety. One  of the main prerequisites of a healthy dialogue   is safety. You cannot have a really constructive  conversation if not all parties feel it's a safe   environment. To maintain that crucial safety, you  need to consider two core elements, what is being   discussed and what is happening in response?  Both content and conditions are important,   and it makes sense when you put yourself in  that situation. If the conditions are safe,   you can say almost anything and it's going to  be perceived semi-okay, even if it's something   really bad. People typically become defensive not  because of what is being said, AKA the content,   but how they feel, or if they feel it's a safe  place. If you know the other person has your   best interest in mind, you have no doubt about  it, you're going to be that much more open to   receiving even truly negative feedback. So how do you make the conditions safe?   Well, there's four parts to it. First is  spot the turning point. That is, notice   when the conversation becomes crucial. That can  be something physical. For instance, a person's   shoulders may tense up. It could be emotional,  when someone becomes angry or afraid or hurt, or   behavioral, if someone raises a voice or becomes  quiet. Two is watch for signs of safety problems.   When people begin to feel unsafe, they may push,  insult, become sarcastic, or make fun of you.   Instead of fighting back, try to see the other  person's aggression as a sign that they don't feel   safe. Be curious, rather than angry or fearful.  Three, see if others are moving towards silence or   verbal violence, and four, beware of  reverting to your own style under stress,   by paying close attention to what you're doing  and the impact it is having. Are you withdrawing   yourself? Are you masking things up with jokes  or sarcasm? Knowing yourself and how you tend to   react under pressure, and trying to improve  on that, is crucial to any conversation.   Next is step number three. You need to make the  content safe. For people to feel safe in speaking   what is really on their minds, two things need  to exist, a common purpose and mutual respect.   Typically, when someone doesn't feel safe saying  something which is potentially negative, but   nevertheless true, it is because of two things.  Either they don't trust the mutual purpose,   and think of the last time you talked to someone  and had a vibe that there's an ulterior motive,   or the mutual respect has been undermined.  And think of the last eye roll that you   received or did, and the dialogue cannot really  resume until that respect has been restored.   Common purpose, mutual respect,  absolutely crucial to any conversation.   So start by asking yourself what do  others believe you care about their goals,   and if they can trust your motives. If you don't  genuinely care, but you're trying to get your way,   quote, unquote, others will quickly see that,  and that destroys the entire conversation.   After that, having respect for the other person  as a human being, and focus on things that make   you similar, rather than different, and  you should be in a much better spot.   Once safety in conditions and content has  been ensured, let's move on to the next part,   and that is controlling your emotions. By learning  to better control your emotions, you'll be in a   much better position to use all the tools we've  covered so far. But what really are emotions?   These are generally the stories with ourselves  when someone does or says something. They're not   forced upon you by others. Others don't make you  mad. You make yourself mad. And it's a bit of a   mind twist, but oh my God, so true. So make sure  that you're in charge of the story that is going   on in your head. Is it the full story? Is it  a true story? By learning to control emotions,   you'll be better positioned to have a successful  crucial conversation. Remember that emotions   don't just happen, and you can either control  your emotions or be controlled by them.   Here's a neat little tactic to help you become  the master of your emotions. It is called   retracing your path to action. It's essentially  going back from how you acted. It goes like this.   First, you start with the act. Examine your  behavior. Ask yourself, how am I acting right   now? Then you move on to the feeling. Identify the  feeling. Ask yourself, what are the exact emotions   that are driving the above behavior? Then you move  on to the story. Ask yourself, what story that   I'm telling myself is creating these emotions?  And finally, examine the facts. Ask yourself,   what is the evidence, things that you see or hear,  that support the story? By retracing your path,   you can see exactly what is going on, hence  gaining control over it in order to change your   emotion, if needed. It is a phenomenal exercise.  It's hard to do it at first, but the more you do   it, the more you're going to discover how powerful  it is in changing your own emotional state.   Step number five is share your stories. Now that  you're the ultimate master of your emotions,   it is time to share your stories in a  way that makes others receptive to them,   in a way that encourages feedback. Share your  facts. Explain what conclusion you're drawing.   Encourage the other person to do the  same, share their story and their facts.   And state your story as a story, not as a fact,  and we've all been guilty of this. Your story   is your story. It is not a fact of life. And  encourage testing. Proactively seek other views   that you can test your theory against. That was about your story. Next,   you need to understand the other side. So  step number six is explore the other's path.   You need to carefully listen and try to understand  the other person's viewpoint. It is not easy,   I know, but it's absolutely essential. Try  to trace their path to action, same as you   did earlier for yourself. Express an interest in  their views, acknowledge their emotions, restate   what you've heard and understood, and if the other  person is holding back, use the priming technique.   Offering a guess as to what they might be thinking  is a way to get the discussion started.   And now, for the final piece of the puzzle, step  number seven, move the conversation to results.   Once everybody contributes the information to a  crucial conversation, the final step is action.   All the conversation effort is dull, unless there  is a plan of action and follow through to achieve   results. Make assignments, who will do what  and when. Follow through. Agree on how and   when you'll follow up on the agreed assignments.  And finally, document. After all this hard work,   don't let your unreliable memory mess  everything up. Write things down.   Now let's get back to our friend, James. If  he knew what he really wanted to get out of   the conversation, he made his girlfriend  feel safe, was in control of his emotions,   and shared his stories and how he got there, and  moved the conversation to results and action,   he would have walked away out of the crucial  conversation like a champ. Now, let's see how   we can use all this information to handle your  next crucial conversation, because whether you   need to have them and be proactive about it, or  you are going to be put in it, it is coming.   Hey, welcome back. So that was crucial  conversations. As you can see, a lot of   information, so let's unpack a little bit before  you get overwhelmed and let's see how can you get   better at communication and interpersonal  skills and those conversations that are   super high stakes. You know how? By practicing  in a non-essential conversation, because imagine,   if you suck, like most of us do in the  everyday communication, there is no way   the crucial conversation is going to happen,  and you're like, "Wait, I usually suck here,   but let me just raise up to the challenge and  just be better." You've got to practice in   the non-essential conversations, in your everyday  conversation with a friend, with a family member,   with a random person on the street. Of course,  be safe out there, but here's how it goes.   It all starts with self awareness. The next  time you have a conversation with somebody,   pay attention to yourself. And I know it's a  little bit weird, but here's what I mean. Pay   attention to how you're behaving. Are you actively  listening? Are you paying attention to what's   going on? Or are you zoning out about a different  topic? If the other person says something that   maybe ticks you off a little bit, do you go on  the defensive and become a little bit silent,   or do you go on the offensive and try to put them  off? Do you mask your own emotions by sarcasm or   by saying a joke because you're uncomfortable? All  these things, everybody behaves differently, but   you need to become aware of what your natural,  normal state is. Because if you don't know what   you do, because all of this is habit, it's  internal, you've taken years to develop it,   most likely you're not even aware of it. So  you need to first bring that awareness up   so you can see what you're doing, so then  you can start taking steps into adjusting   it in whichever direction that is for you. And the more you practice, the more it's going   to become second nature, because that's the way  it goes. A crucial conversation happens. Your   spouse walks in or your boss walks in, and all  of a sudden you're just dropped into the middle   of a life-changing conversation. There's no way  you can be like, "Wait, let me just pull up all   the information that I saw in this book or this  video online." No, it happens fast. You need to   react to that. So the only way to do it is for all  this information to have been internalized. How   do you do that? By practicing, by practicing  the non-essential conversation, by becoming   a better listener every day. So if you're a better  listener or you pay attention to yourself and to   your emotions, and you know how to express  yourself in the everyday conversations, you   can do this in the high-stakes conversations. It's relatively simple, but it's going to uncover   a lot of things that might be uncomfortable,  and that's okay. You're bettering yourself.   That's the way it works. So practice those  skills in the non-essential conversations,   and you're going to become a better  communicator in the crucial conversations   that are going to change your life. And if you want more of the best books   in interpersonal communication, in productivity  and self-help and personal finance, click on the   subscribe button, join the family. There's  a new video coming out each and every week,   but until then, go practice your communication  skills, go practice that self awareness, become   better at the everyday conversations. Have an  amazing day, and I'll see you in the next one.

title: Crucial Conversations for Mastering Dialogue: What to Expect
transcript: Hi, I'm Joseph Granny, co-founder of Crucial Learning and co-author of Crucial Conversations. Whenever you're not getting the results you want, it's likely an important conversation either hasn't happened or hasn't been handled well. At the heart of healthy and high performance organizations are people willing and able to hold crucial conversations. And while cultures of dialogue fuel success, what happens when people don't step up to the crucial conversations they're facing? Our research shows conversation failures in the workplace are both rampant and costly. In our study of 1100 employees, 43% estimated they waste 2 weeks or more ruminating about an unresolved problem at work. And an astounding one in three estimate their inability to speak up in a crucial moment has cost their organization at least $25,000 in lost time and resources. That's where our course, Crucial Conversations for Mastering Dialogue, comes in. For more than 25 years, Crucial Conversations has given people the skills to speak up when the stakes are high, opinions differ, and emotions run strong. The course teaches nine powerful skills that are grounded in decades of social science research. Learners develop these vital skills through instruction, application, practice, group discussion, and self-reflection. Not just theory, for lasting improvement. Our instructional design is every bit as powerful as our content. Here are three reasons why millions of people have turned to crucial conversations for mastering dialogue. First, hands-on skill building. This course doesn't teach by lecture, and there is no death by PowerPoint instruction. Instead, you'll find plenty of engaging exercises that dive into learners real life conversation challenges along with peer practice scenarios to help them put their new skills to the test. In fact, each time a participant learns a new skill, they'll practice it right away. Second, engaging in relatable videos. You'll see correct, near miss, and disastrous ways of holding crucial conversations, and you'll learn from both the successes and failures of others. Let's take a look at a video from the course. Esther, a manager, needs to talk with one of her team members, Leia, about a mistake that impacted a client. Esther wants to know what happened. And as you watch the video, you're going to see Leia become a little defensive. I want you to watch as Esther creates safety for Leia by using a contrasting statement. That's a skill where you clarify what you don't intend followed by what you do intend. >> Hey, how are you? >> Hey, good. How are you? I'm good. Thanks for taking the time to chat. Can you tell me about the Jones account? I understand the client's upset with the design you created. I just wanted to check in with you. What's going on? >> Are you questioning my design skills? >> Oh, no, no, no. That's not it at all. I have no concerns with the quality of your work. Your past work speaks for itself. I'm just trying to figure out if there's a disconnect between you and the client. Well, the design was fine given the specs I was working off of, but it turns out the specs were wrong. >> I want to brainstorm and really think about what could be causing this problem just so that you don't have to go through this again. What do you think? >> I'm sort of nervous to say >> I'm not trying to blame anyone. I'm just trying to address the gap in expectations. >> Okay. Well, usually we go over the design specifications during the pre-call and everything is just fine, but lately Zach we use videos just like this throughout the course to show learners when to use the skills, what it looks like to use the skills, and how using the skills can impact the direction of a conversation. Third, easy to use tools and materials. Our courses come with resources to help learners take their new skills from the classroom to the workplace and even into their personal lives and relationships. We provide job aids, learner guides, and after training reminders to help people put their new skills into action. Crucial conversations for mastering dialogue is also offered in in-person, virtual, and ondemand learning formats. So, the learning experience is convenient and flexible to meet your unique needs. You can even pair on demand with face-to-face instruction for a powerful blended learning experience. If you're looking to reach alignment and agreement, diffuse emotional or politically charged moments, or create a culture where people feel enabled and supported in speaking up about their concerns and opinions, then Crucial Conversations for Mastering Dialogue is for you.
